items.title: The 'extraordinary mitigating circumstances' that spared a grid drop
items.author: Josh Suttill
items.content:
Nico Hulkenberg has held onto his 10th place starting grid position for Formula 1’s Singapore Grand Prix despite having been found to have “unnecessarily impeded” Carlos Sainz in qualifying.

Even Hulkenberg seemed to be expecting a penalty for impeding Sainz as he was on the racing line on the entry to Turn 5 on a cooldown lap, while Sainz was pushing on his final Q2 lap. 

“I don't know, I didn't get told, I thought he was on a cool lap or whatever, I don't know. I didn't have a call - and yeah, doesn't sound great, unfortunately!” Hulkenberg said after qualifying when asked about the investigation. 

Sainz had to abandon his lap and was knocked out in 14th place, with Hulkenberg’s Audi also eliminated in 11th - but George Russell’s grid penalty means he’ll start 10th.

But Hulkenberg's impeding went unpunished because what the stewards described as “extraordinary mitigating circumstances”. 

Audi told the stewards that they believed “based on timing information to which they subscribed, sourced from the official timekeeping provider, that [Sainz] had already taken the chequered flag and conveyed that information to the driver by radio. 

“Therefore [Hulkenberg] did not expect [Sainz] to still be on a push lap when it was closing in. 

“The stewards acknowledge the fact that the data referenced by the team led the team to reasonably believe that [Sainz] had received the chequered flag. Indeed, it was evident from [Sainz’s] radio messages that its team had formed the same belief relying on the same data. 

“The misunderstanding was revealed to be attributable to the information initially received by the teams not being fully synchronised and only being displayed in a correct manner after a short period of time. 

“However, that post-processing did not occur until [Sainz] arrived behind [Hulkenberg], depriving the team of any reasonable opportunity to correct the information conveyed to the driver. 

“In the stewards’ assessment, because the source of the data upon which the team relied was the official timing provider, it was not unreasonable for the team to have relied upon it, even though the team also had available to it the official timing data which conflicted. 

“The stewards determined that Car 55 was unnecessarily impeded. However, there were extraordinary mitigating circumstances in this case because the incident was attributable to the team’s reliance on information that was, for a brief period, inconsistent.” 

Williams team boss James Vowles had said before the judgement was revealed that: “One of the systems indicated that he had crossed the line after the flag, but in reality he hadn’t and we need to make sure we tighten up that process and keep pushing until such time as we are confident.”

items.title: F1 2026 Singapore Grand Prix starting grid after two penalties
items.author: Josh Suttill
items.content:
Max Verstappen and Charles Leclerc will share the front row for Formula 1's Singapore Grand Prix.

Below you'll find the full starting grid after two grid penalties.

George Russell's retirement in Malaysia meant he headed to Singapore knowing he'd need to take a hefty set of grid penalties for taking new power unit components. That total currently stands at 40 places.

He qualified seventh but will still start 21st, ahead of Red Bull's Isack Hadjar, who encountered multiple reliability issues on Saturday and couldn't set a time in qualifying. He was given permission to start the race by the stewards.

Aston Martin revealed it will change the power unit on Fernando Alonso's car, which should mean he'll join Russell and Hadjar at the back, but the FIA is yet to issue official confirmation of any penalty.

items.title: Why driver apologies won't fix McLaren clash
items.author: Jon Noble
items.content:
McLaren boss Andrea Stella is not interested in apologies from his drivers over their “unacceptable” collision in the Singapore Grand Prix sprint race, with post-weekend talks planned to address what he thinks is a “serious” situation.

Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri clashed on the final lap of Saturday’s sprint as they battled for fourth place behind Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc.

Norris had made a move down the inside of Piastri at Turn 5, with the Australian feeling he had left enough room for them both to get through the turn.

Piastri was spun into the wall and retired, while Norris was able to get going again to come home eighth – taking a single point.

The incident upset Stella who, in the team’s post-qualifying press release, labelled throwing away fourth and fifth place like that as “unacceptable.” 

His annoyance was evident when he spoke in the Singapore paddock on Saturday evening.

What irritated him was not just the loss of points that could have an impact on McLaren’s finishing position in the constructors’ championship, but that the drivers had put themselves in a situation where their interests were put ahead of the team.

“It is serious,” said Stella when asked by The Race about how big a situation this was for the team. “It is serious because the damage for the team is material.

“We are in a close fight in the championship. We had the ambition to challenge Ferrari and this is a problem in the challenge to the second position. We have an ambition to finish ahead of Red Bull and this is a problem to finish ahead of Red Bull.

“It is also serious because we come from a few seasons in which we have reflected together, team and drivers, as to how we approach racing together and how we make sure that the interest of the team is protected.”

While Stella spoke to both drivers following the incident, and has vowed to make sure the message is rammed home that they must avoid repeat trouble in the Singapore GP race, it is understood further talks are planned for the gap before the United States Grand Prix in Austin.

Although Norris apologised for his part in the crash because he was the one who instigated the move, Stella thinks the matter goes beyond just saying sorry.

“The aspect of apologies, the fault of one driver, that's not the perspective I have and that's not the perspective I want from the drivers,” he said.

“I want the drivers to take the perspective, and the reflection around this, in how together we are going to pursue, protect, and promote the interest of the team. This is the assignment. I'm not looking forward for any apologies.

“I know the drivers, they are two excellent human beings. But here is business. And as a business, I want to know, and that's the reflection that I want to keep developing, how do we work together to make sure that this does not happen anymore?

“And even more, if possible, the collaboration of the two drivers delivers the best result in the interest of the team.”

While Norris was sorry for what happened, he told media after qualifying that he felt he had the right to gun for the pass of Piastri.

“The gap closed a bit more than I would have liked and obviously I've had to back out of it because the gap was closing,” he told ViaPlay.

“So I've had to try and avoid the incident and obviously there still was one. But it was a big gap so I went for it, I have the right to do that. The rest we go review as a team."

Piastri suggested that the whole situation was unnecessary as the team was on course for a decent points haul.

 “The biggest thing obviously is we just can't have that happen in terms of the points and also the workload and money,” he explained.

“It just wasn't a situation that needed to happen really, so Lando apologised and we moved on.

“Unfortunately it's not our first coming together. I think we're both very good at saying sorry when we need to and moving on, and I think that's what makes us strong as a team.”

McLaren has shown that it is not afraid to take action against drivers in the event of a collision.

After last year’s Singapore Grand Prix, where Norris was judged to have been at fault in a clash with Piastri, the team dished out consequences for Norris in terms of their running order in qualifying for the following race in Austin.

However, that sanction was rolled back almost immediately after Piastri caused a crash at the first corner of the sprint race in Austin.

items.title: How Ferrari handed Singapore pole to Verstappen
items.author: Scott Mitchell-Malm
items.content:
Ferrari's Formula 1 drivers were rightly disappointed to be on the wrong side of a narrow spread in Singapore Grand Prix qualifying as both Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton could have denied Max Verstappen pole.

Just over a tenth of a second separated the trio around the Marina Bay circuit in a Q3 session that had the door left open given Verstappen failed to improve on his final lap - but Leclerc's late leap was not enough, and Hamilton went slower than he had before.

Red Bull finally has a car that Verstappen can hustle to the top spot at the only regular circuit from his F1 career he had not scored a pole or won at prior to this weekend.

But, not to detract from Red Bull's obvious progress, and Verstappen's own quality lap, his description of it being "enough for pole" was exactly right. For he did not have the quickest car in this session and Leclerc, and especially Hamilton, will be lamenting how Q3 played out.

"The car had potential for pole today, but we didn't have a smooth enough session in order to do the job," said Leclerc. "And Max just did a better job."

The Ferrari pair's pole bids failed at different points. For Leclerc, Q3 was a huge salvage job after struggling throughout Q1 and Q2, and the only reason he was in the mix at all was "I just committed a little bit more in Q3 on the last lap".

But it was probably the spectre of braking issues in those sessions that haunted him when it counted, as he conceded it was "taking off quite a lot of confidence".

Bleeding time in the Turn 13 hairpin, where he lost almost a tenth compared to Hamilton with slightly weak rotation, and being too conservative braking for the Turn 16-17 chicane were Leclerc's undoing.

For Turn 16, where Leclerc lost the bulk of his 0.161s deficit to Verstappen in sector three, he just did not attack enough under braking so arrived slightly undercooked - as evidenced by hooking his front right wheel over the inside kerb at a corner you ideally wanted to be just gliding past it along the white line to maximum speed into and through the corner.

But Leclerc was also generally not quite as mighty as Hamilton through the middle sector, where the Ferrari's superiority was unchallenged, so he did not quite gain enough on Verstappen here to offset the weaker final sector. There was perhaps further evidence of his uncertainty under braking: holding a higher gear than Hamilton at a few points around the lap, including leaving it in third for Turns 8 and 14, which Hamilton took in second.

Hamilton has looked a lot more comfortable being so aggressive on corner entry, and was electric through Q1 and Q2. He was much more at one with Ferrari and really extracting the most of its impressive poise under braking and sharp front end into the slower, 90-degree corners especially.

But having been quickest in the first two segments he only managed to go 0.033s quicker in Q3.

"The car felt amazing in Q1 and Q2, and when I finished the laps, I was like, ‘she's got more in her'," he said.

"And the only way in order to try and extract that is to try and add wing. I think it just tipped it over the edge.

"It was only like one hole or something like that. After that the car was just snappy, and none of the laps in Q3 are any good."

Combined they were, though. Hamilton's theoretical best Q3 lap, combining his best sectors, would have been good enough for pole position.

1 Verstappen 1m31.373s2 Leclerc 1m31.427s

Ideal lap - best sectors combined

1 Hamilton 1m31.347s2 Verstappen 1m31.373s

But he was too loose through the opening corners of the first lap and too scrappy in the final sector of the second.

On his first lap, Hamilton shipped 0.271s to Verstappen in sector one. This was by virtue of being slightly wide of the apex into the first corner and then - a legacy of this - having to gather up a small moment through Turn 2 before a much bigger slide followed as he cranked the lock on chucking it into Turn 3.

His middle sector was magnificent, 0.273s quicker than Verstappen. At this point, Hamilton was on for pole - but being ever so slightly hot into Turn 16 just delayed him getting back on the power as he switched back for the second part of the chicane.

On the second run, a tidier first sector and a good but not great middle sector had him in the mix again going into the final part of the lap but an untidy run through 16 and 17 again, with Hamilton sawing at the wheel, meant the lap ended up even slower than the first.

For both drivers, on another day or against a different rival, their small imperfections may not have cost pole. But Verstappen was so strong that he - as he often does - gladly took advantage of others not doing as good a job.

And the Red Bull looked good, too, especially through corners that required a bit more speed on entry. His lap started very purposefully with the front end nice and sharp through the opening sequence of corners and the rear keeping up well. But it was clearly weaker braking and getting the front in for a lot of the 90-degree slower corners in the middle sector, with Verstappen evidently more cautious braking for Turn 7 and then never quite as convincing through the rest of the middle sector.

It came back to him at the end of the lap - and holding third gear to the Ferraris' second into Turn 16 and 17 was perhaps a hint at how both car and driver were just more hooked up there - before ending the lap slightly stronger through the fast final corner too.

"The margins are very close between us throughout the whole of qualifying," said Verstappen.

"So, of course, very happy to be on pole because this is the one that I wanted.

"The car has been pretty strong all weekend. Of course, there are always things that you look into that can be better, but it was enough for pole, so very happy with that."

items.title: Winners and losers from Singapore GP 2026 F1 qualifying
items.author: Josh Suttill
items.content:
A better evening for the championship leader’s upgraded car still wasn’t enough to get Kimi Antonelli and Mercedes into the Singapore Grand Prix pole fight, so it’s turning into a very good weekend for (one) Red Bull.

Here’s our full winners and losers rundown from qualifying.

Winner: Max Verstappen (1st)

Max Verstappen might just be one good start away from finally ending his Singapore hex and taking a grand prix victory on the one remaining circuit he has raced at regularly in F1 without winning.

He’s looked hooked up in the Red Bull this weekend as the 2026 car looks much more suited to the Marina Bay street circuit than its ground-effect predecessors ever did. 

It wasn’t perfect. That Verstappen couldn’t improve on his final run left him vulnerable. But there’s no better place to start from if Verstappen is to make it two wins on the spin: although he’s clearly still not convinced by Red Bull’s startline troubles. 

He was mugged off the line by George Russell in the sprint and Verstappen says there are “no excuses” for this given the sister Racing Bulls team is having good launches with the same software and hardware.

Loser: Isack Hadjar (22nd)

A session that left the other Red Bull driver “pissed off” and wishing he’d stayed at home.

Isack Hadjar commended the work done by his Red Bull mechanics to get him out on track before a gearbox issue that “broke the fourth gear” and caused another abrupt end. 

Hadjar was less than pleased after qualifying ended and went into somewhat of a spiral in his media session about his dislike for the current sprint format, the future sprint races and the “very disappointing” decision-making that led to more sprints being put on the calendar.  

Part of the Red Bull driver’s frustration comes from having his excitement of getting over his handling issues ruined and the chance of points on Sunday now looking far from reality. Or, as he rather amusingly summed up: “I could’ve stayed back in Paris and it would’ve been the same [result.]”

Winner: Upgraded Mercedes (4th)

Kimi Antonelli’s gap to pole was cut from seven tenths to two tenths of a second from Friday to Saturday, a victory for the upgraded Mercedes.

Antonelli said: “We went completely opposite with the set-up [after the sprint race], and the car was in a happier place”. 

The Race understands that the balance shift took the car away from generating too much oversteer and giving Antonelli a lack of confidence under braking. 

Antonelli played around with differential settings during the sprint that dialled a lot of that oversteer out - leading to stronger pace later in the race - and that was followed by major set-up changes after the sprint, including raising the ride height and thus moving the aero balance back into a better window.

He thinks Mercedes should switch both its drivers to the new package for the next race at Austin so the team can keep experimenting to find the right window for its new upgrade. 

Russell, a largely meaningless sixth in qualifying with a hefty engine penalty to serve for the race, wasn’t quite as glowing.

“It was positive to see Kimi more competitive today than yesterday, however, we weren't exactly lighting the timing screen on fire,” Russell said.

“As a team we’re still not satisfied with where we are with the new package. We recognise we need to make set-up adjustments to compensate for those changes. Maybe we can find a way to make it work, but right now we need more time.”

The upgraded Mercedes is still lagging behind the Red Bull and the Ferrari in Singapore at least, but it’s clearly made a step in the right direction.

Loser: Aston Martin (17th + 19th)

A messy session that may leave Aston Martin even worse off than the initial qualifying results suggest. 

Fernando Alonso already suggested he may take a grid penalty for a turbo issue that progressively worsened throughout Saturday’s action, culminating in a loss of power and momentum on the exits of the corners and a Q1 exit. 

A lockup and a little bit of traffic were the story on the other side of the garage, as Lance Stroll surmised that the main Aston Martin issue comes from the bumpy nature of the Marina Bay circuit not working for its current package.

Given the track conditions are unlikely to change overnight, and the low grid positions could get even lower, the reality is a far cry from the pre-event aspirations of another potential points haul.

Winner: Charles Leclerc (2nd)

After a bruising sprint where he faded badly with front tyre wear, this was Charles Leclerc at his best - dancing through discomfort to pull a very good qualifying lap out from nowhere.

He lagged badly behind Ferrari team-mate Lewis Hamilton in Q1 and Q2, struggling with the car pulling to one side under braking, but with more “commitment” he turned the tables in Q3 and even got surprisingly close to pole.

Leclerc suggested he still wasn’t entirely happy with the car so, even beyond a front-row start typically being a good qualifying result, this worked out very well.

Loser: Lewis Hamilton (3rd)

Context is critical for establishing why Hamilton ultimately lost out in qualifying. 

Third on the grid is fine, especially when the gaps were so small. But it could have been so much more. 

Leclerc said there was more in the Ferrari and Hamilton was the evidence. His theoretical best lap in Q3 was quicker than Verstappen’s, so if he had pieced together the sectors, he would be first. Plain and simple. 

Hamilton had been delighted with his runs through Q1 and Q2 so to have that final outcome, after a Q3 in which he said neither lap was any good, is a loss. -

Loser: Franco Colapinto (16th)

Eight places down on Alpine team-mate Pierre Gasly was more like the Franco Colapinto of old, rather than the driver who has been on terms with Gasly for much of the second half of the season. 

Colapinto ended up in the wall in Q2 at Turn 17 but even before then he wasn’t looking likely to join Gasly in Q3. 

“It's very strange,” Colapinto said of his 16th place. “Before the wall, I was already a lot slower than my Q1 lap, which normally you would improve a lot. 

“So, I don't know, very strange, I had no rear grip the last lap. It was extremely poor, it was the worst balance I've had in the weekend. 

“So, I don't know, a bit lost, to be honest, because Q1 felt quite easy to do the lap and it was coming not too bad, but then it was very, very poor.”

Winner: Pierre Gasly (8th)

For the third consecutive grand prix qualifying session, Gasly won F1’s midfield battle, beating both Racing Bulls in Q3.

Gasly called it “one of my best Q3s of the year” in a season he took pole at Monza, as he was thrilled with his execution on a sprint weekend.

He’s just hoping his Q3 appearance will translate into points, unlike in Azerbaijan and Malaysia.

“I must say the last few weekends, I think we have done four Q3s [including Singapore sprint] in the last four quali, but somehow we haven't scored that much because it's always gone wrong for whatever reason,” Gasly said.

“So as much as I would like a bit of chaos tomorrow, [it’s] hopefully not involving us another time, and hopefully we can translate this good quali into points.”

Alex Albon was half a second slower than Williams team-mate Carlos Sainz in Q1 despite being “relatively happy with my lap”.

The data suggests the majority of that loss seems to come with the way Albon approached the tricky Turn 13 left-hander.

Team boss James Vowles said Albon “wasn’t as comfortable in the car” after Williams made repairs following the sprint, in which he shunted into the back of Gabriel Bortoleto’s Audi at the safety car restart. 

Sainz’s Q2 was also compromised as Williams’s systems indicated he’d taken the chequered flag when he actually hadn’t - so he abandoned his lap and with it any chance of beating the Haas drivers. 

“We will have a look overnight and see what changes we need to do so both drivers can come back stronger tomorrow,” Vowles said. -

items.title: Verstappen beats Ferraris to Singapore GP pole
items.author: Josh Suttill
items.content:
Max Verstappen’s perfect Singapore weekend continued as he claimed pole position for the grand prix, beating the Ferraris in Formula 1 qualifying.

Verstappen’s first Q3 flying lap - a 1m31.373s - ended up being good enough to top qualifying, following on from his sprint race pole and victory.

Charles Leclerc’s Ferrari was his closest challenger, setting a lap 0.054s slower than Verstappen’s. Lewis Hamilton made it two Ferraris in the top three, just 0.069s adrift of Leclerc.

Kimi Antonelli will line up on the second row alongside Hamilton, having been fourth-quickest in the upgraded Mercedes.

The McLaren drivers, who collided in the sprint race, will share the third row.

Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri were fifth and seventh in qualifying with George Russell between them in the older-spec Mercedes, but Russell will move to the back of the grid with an engine penalty.

Pierre Gasly won F1’s midfield fight in qualifying, qualifying eighth (which is set to become seventh on the grid) and beating the Racing Bulls duo of Liam Lawson and Arvid Lindblad.

Audi’s Nico Hulkenberg was the quickest driver knocked out in Q2, 0.182s away from a place in Q3.

Haas drivers Ollie Bearman and Esteban Ocon were 12th and 13th ahead of Carlos Sainz’s Williams, Audi’s Gabriel Bortoleto and Alpine’s Franco Colapinto, over a second slower than team-mate Gasly.

Both Aston Martins fell in the first stage of qualifying after Fernando Alonso reported a turbo issue, which he thinks means his team should change his power unit for the race.

He qualified 17th, just ahead of Alex Albon’s Williams and still seven tenths clear of team-mate Lance Stroll, just as he was in sprint qualifying.

Sergio Perez led Cadillac team-mate Valtteri Bottas, the pair the two slowest drivers to set a lap in qualifying.

Isack Hadjar’s nightmare Saturday in Singapore continued as he ground to a halt before he could even set a timed lap in Q1.

Hadjar managed to return his Red Bull to the garage, then came out again and encountered an issue again. He will start among the penalised drivers at the back of the field on Sunday.

items.title: Stewards rule Piastri shares blame for Norris clash
items.author: Josh Suttill
items.content:
Formula 1’s Singapore Grand Prix stewards determined that both Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri contributed to their last-lap sprint race collision, so ruled that no further action was necessary.

The stewards said Piastri hadn’t expected Norris to overtake him, but he "noticed [Norris] on the inside and attempted to leave space".

"[Norris] said that he saw an opportunity to overtake and said that the front axle of his car was ahead of the mirror of [Piastri] prior to the apex, and therefore expected to be left space.

"As he approached the apex, the space was less than he had anticipated, so he had to use the inside kerb and braked, and a collision occurred.

"The stewards considered that both drivers had contributed to the incident and that neither driver was wholly or predominantly to blame for the collision.

"Therefore, the stewards determined to take no further action."

Norris is right that he had his front axle ahead of the mirror of Piastri’s sister car at the apex of Turn 5, so he satisfies that aspect of F1’s racing rules.

But it does not appear Piastri - who was caught unawares by the divebomb - had means of leaving more space at that corner; so once he turned in, a collision became inevitable.

Given the stewards stated "both drivers had contributed to the incident", we can infer that Piastri’s not anticipating the overtake and leaving enough space is what he did wrong - whereas Norris was ambitious with his move and had to climb onto the inside kerb to try to complete it.

The start of Norris’s interview with F1 broadcaster Viaplay after the sprint race made his feelings clear.

Norris was asked: "You'll surely always want to finish as high as possible, but it’s also a sprint, P4 and P5 and it was your team-mate in front of you... Wasn’t it too unnecessary, that move?"

He replied: "What, to go for a big gap? To overtake?". He followed up: "What's the title name of the race?"

The interviewer replied, "sprint", to which Norris said: "Sprint. What’s [the word] after sprint?" - "race" came the reply.

Norris smiled: "Wow! Good job. It’s a race".

"We were just stuck the whole race and the last lap there was a big opportunity into [Turn] 5 so I went for it," Norris said in the media pen.

"The gap closed a bit more than I would have liked and obviously I've had to back out of it because the gap was closing - so I've had to try and avoid the incident and obviously there still was one. But it was a big gap so I went for it, I have the right to do that. The rest we go review as a team."

Piastri said "it’s for fourth and fifth for a sprint race, not that bothered either way, just a lot of work for the team to get both cars fixed, just a shame for the team".

Meanwhile, Liam Lawson, having been shown a replay of the incident by Sky Sports F1’s Karun Chandhok, mused: "On the last lap, it’s not for many points; I don't think it's worth it".

Perez dodges serving penalty for Stroll clash

There was a slightly unusual decision made in the assessment of another of the sprint’s incidents.

Sergio Perez and Lance Stroll collided on the opening lap of the race when Perez tried to pass on the inside of the Turn 16 right-hander.

The stewards felt Stroll had turned in reasonably for the corner and Perez was predominantly to blame after having a lock-up.

They considered the tricky conditions reasonable mitigation and wanted to issue Perez with a five-second penalty instead of the usual 10.

But Perez retired from the race - and according to the stewards a five-second penalty does not typically convert to a grid drop.

Had it been a 10-second penalty, this would be different. So Perez escapes sanction for the clash.

items.title: Winners and losers from F1's wet Singapore GP sprint race
items.author: Scott Mitchell-Malm
items.content:
But that still demanded cool heads of the 22 drivers - some of whom were more successful at keeping cool than others.

Here's our pick of winners and losers from the sixth and final sprint race of the 2026 Formula 1 season.

“I just misjudged it,” George Russell said of his early race-ending Singapore crash.

Even if this is likely to make no difference to his ever-dwindling title hopes, Russell is in a position where, for his own sake, he needs to end the year on a high.

Grabbing the lead from Verstappen at the start in the sprint looked like the perfect way to do that before a grid penalty hobbles the rest of his weekend.

But the heavy crash - which he put down to having more power than expected from the battery exiting the final corner and then touching the white line as he ran a little wide - put paid to that in a very painful way.

“It's a very, very silly mistake,” he said. “Overly confident. Think it's my first crash of the year. It's annoying to happen from that position.”

Winner: Kimi Antonelli (4th)

This was a quintessential ‘when it’s your year, it’s your year’ kind of day for Kimi Antonelli.

He did nothing remarkable - which in itself is good because evidently these were conditions it was easy to trip up in - and yet took another little step towards his world championship.

His chief title ‘rival’ Russell crashed out of a winning position on the first lap. Then, at the very end, two cars ahead of him were removed by a needless collision.

Apart from keeping the car on the road this is the easiest progress Antonelli will make all season - and it almost ended in an unlikely sprint podium, such was Leclerc’s trouble by the end of the race.

Loser: McLaren (8th & 14th)

A frustrating but solid race turned into a needlessly destructive one for McLaren thanks to Lando Norris’s over-ambitious final lap move.

Sending it down the inside of Turn 5 in the wet is borderline desperate at the best of times, let alone against your team-mate.

McLaren chiefs must have been holding their breath when it happened but ultimately, while gutted, surely not surprised that it caused a synchronised pirouette from the pair, ending Oscar Piastri’s race in the process.

It was always likely to end badly and it could yet get worse if Norris cops a penalty for it that loses him eighth place, and with it the measly point McLaren still got as a weak silver lining.

Winner: Max Verstappen (1st)

Would Verstappen have had anything to come back at Russell with? We'll never know - though you could infer that Verstappen might've found it difficult considering his assertion post-race that "I think we shouldn't host a sprint where you can't pass".

That's all academic. Verstappen never looked under threat from behind, and his drive to victory had an air of cruise control to it - at a track, too, where Verstappen can struggle to reach his peak level of performance.

Yet more evidence that the four-time champion is the form driver right now.

Loser: Isack Hadjar (DNF)

It's hard to judge Hadjar too harshly considering he managed only two laps before parking up with a power issue.

But he did lose two places at the start, if we're being ultra-critical.

And of course, there's no escaping the fact this was a DNF in a race won by the sister car.

Winner: Lewis Hamilton (2nd)

Lewis Hamilton did the hard work for his sprint race in the opening few seconds, leaping forward past his team-mate and the two McLarens.

Considering he seemed to have the best pace of anyone besides Verstappen in this race, that was critical. Getting stuck on a track where it looked almost impossible to overtake in these conditions - barring bigger pace swings in the midfield - would have made Hamilton’s sprint look a lot more average.

He couldn't quite match Verstappen in the middle of the race but started to whittle away at the lead again late on and was much, much better managing his tyres than team-mate Leclerc seemed to be as the track dried.

Winner: Liam Lawson (5th)

If you can keep your head when all around you are losing theirs...

OK, the Singapore sprint wasn't the most difficult to navigate in reality, but there was still plenty of reward to be reaped from keeping it neat and tidy.

This was another exemplary drive from Lawson, who in repeating his best-of-the-rest trick from qualifying also stood to gain from any incidents up ahead. (Hello, McLaren.)

It's this sort of drive that means the direction of travel is only going one way in the fight for fifth in the constructors' championship between Racing Bulls and Alpine right now.

Loser: Arvid Lindblad (13th)

Compare Lawson's serene run to fifth with Racing Bulls team-mate Lindblad's travails.

Lindblad was perplexed after the race by his spin under the safety car - "it was a bit confusing at the time because it was pretty gentle on power, then just suddenly lost it" - but was a little loose in his description of events that "then I tried to just get it back round", as he in fact had spent multiple seconds driving the car backwards while trying to loop around at Turn 5.

No surprise then that that caught the attention of race control.

And even if he escapes penalty, this was a last-on-the-road finish in the same car that finished well up the road in fifth. There's no question, considering the attrition, that points were up for grabs.

Loser: Cadillac (DNF & DNF)

Two cars. Two collisions. One unproductive race.

The Sergio Perez-Lance Stroll clash looked like as clear a case of racing incident as you'll find, so there's little blame to be apportioned to the Cadillac driver there.

Valtteri Bottas doesn't get such an easy ride. What initially looked like a lazy slide from Alex Albon into the back of Gabriel Bortoleto was actually the result of Bottas getting into the back of the Williams. All this before the race had restarted, too.

The "rubber band" effect was partly to blame - Bottas said "the two cars ahead of me came to full stop and I just didn't have time to react" - but he did ultimately trigger contact.

So much for this being the sort of weekend, and track, that can play into Cadillac's hands...

Winner: Ollie Bearman (6th)

Ollie Bearman was absolutely thrilled with his work in the sprint, even though he acknowledged his seven-place rise was bolstered by others screwing up.

Irrespective of the Russell shunt and McLaren collision, though, Bearman was a man on the move here. He toughed it out nicely to get ahead of Pierre Gasly once the race resumed post-safety car, and that was critical for consolidating a points finish.

Bearman was on course to grab eighth irrespective of what happened on the final lap - so the bump up to sixth merely boosted the Haas driver rather than flattered his efforts completely.

items.title: Verstappen wins delayed Singapore sprint, Russell crashes from lead
items.author: Scott Mitchell-Malm
items.content:
Max Verstappen won an attritional Formula 1 Singapore Grand Prix sprint race bookended by initial race leader George Russell crashing out and the two McLarens colliding.

After a delayed start due to heavy rain in the build-up to the sprint, Russell jumped Verstappen into the first corner - but his lead barely lasted a full lap.

The Mercedes driver, for whom a win might have barely kept alive his faint title hopes, spun exiting the final corner and crashed into the pitwall just beyond the timing line.

That freed up Verstappen to take a controlled victory (after a safety car period) in which he steadily built his lead over Lewis Hamilton and managed it easily until the end.

Hamilton’s second place was earned from a lightning start that vaulted him ahead of both McLarens and his Ferrari team-mate Charles Leclerc.

And he was clearly the faster Ferrari in these conditions as Leclerc faded extremely badly late on, putting him under pressure from Oscar Piastri, Lando Norris and a muted championship leader Kimi Antonelli.

Leclerc looked to have done enough to stave off the McLaren threat even before they collided calamitously on the final lap.

Norris launched a silly move on his team-mate into the Turn 5 right-hander. Piastri left some room on the inside but Norris, who went over the kerb, hit his team-mate's car and spun both of them round.

Though Norris rejoined after a short delay and claimed a point in eighth - a point he may lose given the incident is under investigation - Piastri retired in the wall.

This gifted Antonelli fourth and elevated several midfield cars into healthy points positions.

Liam Lawson spearheaded this group with a very accomplished drive to fifth while Ollie Bearman was sixth for Haas - keeping Nico Hulkenberg from his team’s championship rival Audi at bay in the process.

Hulkenberg had robustly passed Pierre Gasly earlier in the race to run behind Bearman but looked set to end the sprint empty-handed before McLaren imploded.

Among the nine retirees were also Isack Hadjar and Franco Colapinto, who suffered stoppages during the early safety car period, first-lap colliders Lance Stroll and Sergio Perez, and Alex Albon, Gabriel Bortoleto and Valtteri Bottas.

Albon and Bortoleto collided ahead of the safety car period ending in an incident that will be investigated after the race.

items.title: Sprint start crash causes huge tension within Aprilia
items.author: Valentin Khorounzhiy
items.content:
Raul Fernandez has repeatedly excoriated Aprilia stablemate Marco Bezzecchi for his role in setting up their crash at the start of the Mandalika sprint, describing Bezzecchi's tactics as "not nice", "ungentlemanly" and "not clever".

Fernandez fractured his left index finger in the crash at the start of the sprint, which was triggered as four riders - Fernandez, Bezzecchi, Marc Marquez and Fabio Di Giannantonio - went into Turn 1 almost side-by-side and their lines converged deep into the corner.

As Di Giannantonio ran Marquez out wide, Bezzecchi checked up and had contact with Fernandez that took both out of the race and injured the latter. Fernandez is now in doubt for the grand prix, but will try to contest the warm-up.

Fernandez was seething after the sprint, giving explosive interviews to both Spanish broadcaster DAZN and Italian broadcaster Sky Sport, in which he effectively accused Bezzecchi of deliberately compromising his race at the cost of letting two Ducatis through.

His tone softened between the TV interviews and the written media, but his argument remained the same. Bezzecchi, he felt, approached Turn 1 with the focus only on beating Fernandez, squeezed him out and left the door open for the two Ducatis, which created the conditions for the crash.

"For me, the crash is a consequence of the start," Fernandez said. "On the start, for me I tried to keep my bike in the middle of the track, to try to not open the door for other riders to overtake. Marco had made a really good start and he overtook me - he didn't really overtake 100 percent, but he put the bike close to me and started to take me out the track.

"And this is for me the more frustrating thing about today. When you want to do something that is not clean in this sport. We are riders, we put our body [on the line] at more than 300km/h and when you are doing something that you know that is not really nice, I am not happy with that.

"And for me the version is, OK, we crash, it doesn't matter, it can happen, one day it will be me that I will make a mistake, another day will be another rider. The problem is when you are making something that you know is not nice. And for me this is the big problem that we saw today.

"We go out [wide] he doesn't give me space, two Ducatis overtook us, we crash, that's it."

Fernandez chuckled that it was "for sure not good" as a strategy by Bezzecchi. He said the Aprilia riders knew the battle for victory would play out between them, and accused Bezzecchi of "thinking just of me".

"I am not playing for the championship. He was playing for the championship. For me he was not very smart."

He also indicated he was more upset with Bezzecchi over this than with Jorge Martin over the Balaton Park pile-up at Turn 1, as that had been a mere mistake and this was a premeditated "bad action to another rider".

He said it was nothing that could or should be penalised but that Bezzecchi "didn't have the respect" and that, while Aprilia riders are told to be "gentlemen" with one another in terms of wheel-to-wheel racing, it "looks like he [Bezzecchi] was not a gentleman with us".

Bezzecchi defends himself

Bezzecchi was told of Fernandez's incandescence but chalked it up to heat-of-the-moment emotions clouding Fernandez's judgment. "I am maybe the one who can confirm this more than anyone," he joked, in seeming reference to his ban at Assen for striking a marshal.

It was a "racing incident", Bezzecchi insisted. "I was just looking to put myself in the best place possible for the braking. I knew Marc could try to overtake but was for me useless to try to force too much and maybe throw away the race in the first corner.

"It's what I did. If Raul is angry, I'm sorry, but honestly, he touched me! So at the end there's nothing to be angry for. Me versus him or him versus me, at the end it was a racing incident. I couldn't disappear and he also couldn't disappear. I don't want to waste energy with this, I want to focus for tomorrow."

How the Ducati pair saw it

Marquez, who went on to win the sprint, said the incident was "easy to explain".

"Four bikes in parallel, and I believe that Bezzecchi was looking at Raul, to brake a bit later, I was looking at Bezzecchi to brake a bit later, and Diggia was looking at me to brake a bit later. The consequence - four riders out of the line and [Jorge] Martin from fifth to first," he recounted.

Di Giannantonio had been completely unaware that anyone had crashed - but did say that contact with Marquez coming through the corner caused a downshift on his end that then compromised his exit from Turn 1.

"Honestly, you have to ask the others [about the incident] - me, I just got hit again."

items.title: Why Martin had to give up MotoGP sprint win
items.author: Valentin Khorounzhiy
items.content:
MotoGP's former championship leader Jorge Martin had to surrender the Mandalika sprint win and points lead due to the risk of a tyre pressure infringement.

After an opening-corner melee removed fellow Aprilia riders Raul Fernandez and Marco Bezzecchi from the picture, and gave Martin 'free' passage into first from fifth on the grid, the Aprilia man looked to be in control and en route to a comfortable victory.

But Martin suddenly slowed and allowed title rival Marc Marquez through, in a move that looked like a bid to get some heat onto his front tyre and avoid a ruinous eight-second penalty for non-compliance.

The front tyre must be kept above the baseline pressure - around 1.8 bar, though it varies slightly from round to round - for at least 30% of the total laps in the sprint - and Martin confirmed after the race that this was indeed the reason why he had to abandon the lead.

His attempts to then strike back on Marquez came to naught, and a mistake on the penultimate lap dropped him to fourth place - turning what was set to be a five-point lead over Marquez exiting the race into a four-point deficit.

"I didn't do a great start but they were four[-wide] into first corner so it was easy for me to go into the lead," Martin recounted. "Then I tried to push and I was able to make a big gap to Marc. But then I realised that I was under the pressure [requirement]. I tried to push the front more, tried to warm it a bit more, but it wasn't into the [legal] zone.

"So I had to let Marc past, and then after that everything started to get a bit difficult. Even if I was trying to be close [to Marquez] to make a move into the last lap - that's why I made a mistake with two laps to go, and then the chances were gone."

Martin felt that he still carried a "big opportunity" into Sunday to re-assert himself in the championship race.

"For sure tomorrow Marco [Bezzecchi] and [Raul] Fernandez will be super strong - but so will I," he said, albeit perhaps unaware that Fernandez is believed to have sustained a hand injury in the Turn 1 crash.

Why was the pressure too low?

Martin and his crew chief Daniele Romagnoli may not have expected to lead the race - given he was fifth on the grid, and didn't necessarily have the pace to easily clear his fellow Aprilias.

But Martin insisted they didn't set the front tyre pressure particularly low in the expectation of running in the pack.

"It's not a thing that we normally do. We never risk with the tyre pressure, I don't know why today we were out [of the limit].

"I think here it's quite difficult with the humidity, and maybe it changed from yesterday. But honestly we didn't risk.

"Sometimes it happens. It hasn't happened to me a lot in the last few years, but today [it has]. So for sure it's something we need to check, because it's something that today maybe 0.1 [bar higher] I was able to win the same and not be in trouble."

items.title: Marquez takes MotoGP points lead after Aprilia implosion
items.author: Valentin Khorounzhiy
items.content:
Marc Marquez took an unlikely victory in the Indonesian Grand Prix sprint race after a first-corner incident took out two other victory contenders and a series of problems for title rival Jorge Martin.

Martin appeared to be coasting to victory but had to cede position to Marquez and then made a mistake that dropped him off the podium.

With Fabio Di Giannantonio attacking for the lead into Turn 1 on the inside and Marquez trying to squeeze in between the VR46 rider and the Aprilias of Marco Bezzecchi and Raul Fernandez, it was close to a four-wide situation at the start - and it ended in disaster for half of the participants.

With Di Giannantonio taking a late-braking Marquez wide, Bezzecchi picked up the bike and ended up making contact with Fernandez on the outside, both going down as a result.

That first-corner dynamic meant Martin waltzed past, with sudden open road in front of him, to take the lead - and over the first few laps he stretched out a lead of over a second back to Marquez.

But he then slowed suddenly to deliberately wave Marquez back through, in what was presumably a bid to artificially raise his front tyre pressure and avoid a penalty for non-compliance.

This would tally, as Martin and his crew may have set his tyre pressures expecting to run in traffic, but instead he was into the lead from Turn 1.

Once Marquez was handed the lead, Martin quickly pushed back up towards him but struggled to line up any kind of move - and ran off-track on the penultimate lap to relegate himself to fourth place.

Instead, Ai Ogura and Di Giannantonio completed the podium.

It means Marquez now leads Martin by four points in the standings, with Bezzecchi 59 off the lead after his retirement.

Alex Marquez, Pedro Acosta, Fermin Aldeguer, Pecco Bagnaia and Fabio Quartararo rounded out the points - Acosta having served a long-lap penalty for track limits that dropped him from fifth and in-between the Gresini riders.
